title: Snapshot
body:
Few Japanese industrial stocks have moved the way 3103.T has. Between 2021 and 2026, shares in Unitika Ltd. fell to a five-year low of ¥127, then surged to ¥3,745 — a roughly 30-fold intra-period swing that is less a story of business performance than of distress, state-backed rescue, and the market's unresolved verdict on what comes next. As of May 22, 2026, the stock trades at ¥1,574, implying a market capitalisation of ¥90.75 billion on 57.65 million shares outstanding. The beta sits at 2.03. The 52-week range alone — ¥140 to ¥4,380 — captures how violently the market is still renegotiating a fair value.

## What Unitika Actually Makes

The company is not a household name even in Japan. Unitika produces nylon and polyester films used in food packaging and electronics, engineering plastics and resins, glass fabrics and beads for industrial and electronic applications, activated carbon fibers for air and water purification, and nonwoven textiles for agricultural and automotive markets. None of these businesses face the consumer directly; most sit deep in supply chains where Unitika's products are components, not brands. Trailing twelve-month revenue stands at ¥118.56 billion, generated by 2,663 employees — a consolidated workforce roughly 40 per cent smaller than it was in 2013.

## 137 Years and Still Restructuring

The company was established on June 19, 1889, in Hyogo prefecture — founded by Osaka merchants and bankers as Amagasaki Spinners Ltd., a cotton-spinning concern that grew to more than 27,000 spindles within six years. A century of consolidation and reinvention followed: Dainippon Spinning in 1918, then Nichibo in 1964, then — via a 1969 merger with Nippon Rayon Company — the modern Unitika Ltd. That merger planted the strategic seeds of today's film and fiber portfolio. What it could not resolve was the secular decline of Japan's textile industry, which has been Unitika's central problem for half a century.

## The REVIC Moment

On April 30, 2025, Unitika's board cancelled all outstanding Class A and Class B preferred shares and issued new Class C preferred shares to the Regional Economic Vitalization Corporation of Japan (REVIC) via a ¥20 billion third-party allotment. The transaction handed REVIC 66.76 per cent of voting rights. At the same board meeting, Fujii Minoru — a career Unitika employee since 1987 — was appointed President and Representative Director. Three of Japan's major lenders — MUFG, Mizuho, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust — simultaneously approved debt forgiveness of up to ¥43 billion. The ¥20 billion in fresh capital was earmarked precisely: ¥14 billion to fund withdrawal from unprofitable businesses, ¥6 billion for demolition of surplus facilities.

REVIC is not a conventional investor. Established after the 2011 earthquake to revitalise regional enterprises, its presence signals that Unitika is considered systemically significant enough to rescue — but also that private capital was unwilling to lead.

## From Impairment to Operating Recovery

The financial trajectory explains the stock chart. In the fiscal year ended March 2025, Unitika booked a [¥37.9 billion impairment charge](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/pdf/fin-may142025.pdf), writing down the carrying value of businesses it has since either sold or placed on the exit list. The resulting net loss was ¥24.3 billion on revenue of ¥126.4 billion, and the equity ratio fell to 10.4 per cent — a figure that, in a capital-intensive manufacturer, approaches the threshold of technical distress.

The nine months to December 2025 tell a starkly different story. Revenue reached ¥95.6 billion (+2.2 per cent year-on-year), operating profit hit ¥9.03 billion — a 110.3 per cent increase against the prior-year ¥4.3 billion — and net income flipped from a ¥24.4 billion loss to a ¥10.6 billion gain. The equity ratio recovered to 25.2 per cent, supported by the REVIC injection and ¥23.7 billion in gains from asset disposals. Cash ballooned by ¥44.5 billion to ¥57.96 billion. Full-year FY3/26 guidance, revised in February 2026, projects net income of ¥20 billion — on revenue of just ¥110 billion, deliberately smaller as divested units roll off the consolidation perimeter.

## Turnaround or Controlled Liquidation?

The headline numbers look good. But they also crystallise the question that the rest of this report will attempt to answer. Unitika's own five-year plan, filed alongside the restructuring disclosure, projects revenue of ¥70 billion by FY3/29 — a 45 per cent reduction from the FY3/25 base — with operating profit of ¥6.5 billion. The company is, by its own design, becoming substantially smaller. Whether the remaining core — polymer films, technical glass fibers, activated carbon — constitutes a viable, independently owned business, or whether the endgame is an orderly wind-down and piecemeal asset transfer, is the question REVIC, the banks, and Unitika's minority shareholders are all watching Fujii Minoru to answer.
